Learning Objectives
Appropriately evaluate patients with metatarsus adductus.
Assess the natural history of metatarsus adductus and determine the optimal timing of
surgical management.
Interpret the differential diagnosis for metatarsus adductus and the defining feature that
differentiates metatarsus adductus from other diagnoses.
Evaluate patients with a calcaneovalgus foot and differentiate a calcaneovalgus foot from
other diagnoses.
Interpret the natural history of calcaneovalgus foot deformities.
Assess and determine underlying conditions associated with calcaneovalgus foot deformity.

Metatarsus Adductus
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Intrauterine positioning of the foot is a possible cause of metatarsus adductus.
Metatarsus adductus is a medial deviation of the forefoot with neutral to mild valgus
alignment of the hindfoot.
Epidemiology
Occurs in as many as 12% of newborns
One of the most common foot deformity in newborns, representing three-quarters of all foot
abnormalities at birth

Epidemiology
Metatarsus adductus was first described by Henke in 1863.1 Along with calcaneovalgus
foot deformity, metatarsus adductus is one of the most common foot deformities in
newborns, representing three-quarters of all foot abnormalities.2 Metatarsus adductus
is common in the sibling of an individual with metatarsus adductus. It also is more
common in twins, males, and preterm babies. The condition more frequently occurs on
the left side.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The medial cuneiform is abnormally shaped in some patients with metatarsus adductus (ie, it
is trapezoidal with a broadened and medially tilted articular surface at the metatarsal-medial
cuneiform articulation);2 however, normal bony structure may be observed.
Tendons

Some studies suggest that metatarsus adductus is caused by an anomalous insertion of the
tibialis anterior tendon.
Joints and Ligaments
Joints and ligaments are normal.
Musculature
Some studies suggest that metatarsus adductus is caused by a muscle imbalance from a tight
anterior tibial tendon.
Other studies refute this etiology because metatarsus adductus is not commonly observed in
patients with underlying neurologic conditions that cause muscle imbalance across the
midfoot.
Etiology
Intrauterine malpositioning is a possible cause of this deformity.2
Classification
The Bleck classification system grades the severity of deformity according to flexibility. A
flexible forefoot can be abducted beyond the midline heel-bisector line, and a partially flexible
forefoot can be abducted to the midline; however, a rigid forefoot cannot be abducted to the
midline3 (Figure 1; Resource 1).

Figure 1 Illustrations of feet show the classification of metatarsus adductus using the heel-
bisector line, which defines the relationship of the heel to the forefoot. (Reproduced from
Scaduto AA, Frost NL: Pediatric foot conditions, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
1413-1422.)

Etiology
Metatarsus adductus is thought to result from intrauterine positioning. Anatomic
variation is another theory because surgical findings have indicated that muscle
imbalance from a tight anterior tibial tendon or anomalous insertion of this tendon
causes metatarsus adductus; however, other studies do not support this theory because
metatarsus adductus is not commonly observed in patients with muscle imbalance (eg,
cerebral palsy). In some patients, an abnormally shaped medial cuneiform (ie,
trapezoidal rather than rectangular) with a broadened and medially tilted articular
surface at the metatarsal-medial cuneiform articulation has been noted.2
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Metatarsus Adductus and Calcaneovalgus Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000032
4/17

Metatarsus adductus is associated with other packing disorders, such as developmental
dysplasia of the hip (DDH) and torticollis. A 1982 study of 720 infants with metatarsus
adductus reported a 1.53% incidence of DDH,4 whereas a more recent study reported a
co-incidence of 4%.3 Both of these rates exceed the rate of DDH in the general
population, highlighting the need to fully evaluate all patients with metatarsus adductus
for DDH.
Normally, a line bisecting the heel passes through the second toe or between the second
and third toes. Metatarsus adductus is considered mild if the heel-bisector line crosses
the third toe, moderate if the heel-bisector line crosses between the third and fourth
toes, and severe if the heel-bisector line crosses between the fourth and fifth toes.3
Evaluation/Diagnosis
The foot has a kidney bean shape (convex lateral border), and the hindfoot is in a neutral to
mild valgus position.
The amount of active deformity correction is assessed by stroking the lateral border of the foot
to elicit firing of the peroneal tendons.
Physical Examination
Together, the adducted forefoot and the curved lateral border create a kidney bean–shaped
sole.
The fifth metatarsal base may be prominent.
The hindfoot is in neutral or slight valgus alignment.
Hyperactivity of the abductor hallucis may contribute to the dynamic component of deformity.
Abduction of the great toe may be observed.
Mild plantar flexion deformity of the medial column leads to the appearance of an elevated
arch.
Flexibility is assessed by abducting the forefoot relative to the hindfoot.
In young patients, stroking the lateral border of the foot to elicit active correction may help
determine the flexibility of the deformity.
Later in life, pressure sores may be present under the first metatarsophalangeal joint or the
base of the fifth metatarsal base.

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs rarely are indicated.
Radiographs may be obtained in patients with a rigid deformity and patients in whom
nonsurgical treatment fails; ideally, radiographs are obtained with the patient bearing weight
(Figure 2).
Radiographs may reveal the following:
Obliquity of the medial cuneiform
Adduction of the metatarsals at the level of the tarsometatarsal joint
Medial deviation of the metatarsal shafts, especially in older children
Figure 2 Images show skewfoot. A, Clinical photograph of the feet of a patient with skewfoot. B,
AP radiograph of the foot of a patient with skewfoot demonstrates hindfoot valgus, talar plantar
flexion, midfoot abduction, and forefoot adduction. (Courtesy of Erin M. Honcharuk, MD,
Baltimore, MD.)
Differential Diagnosis
Clubfoot
Hyperactive abductor hallucis

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000032
6/17

Internal tibial torsion
Skewfoot
Metatarsus primus varus
Bracket epiphysis of the first metatarsal

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Parents may bring in their newborn with concerns about cosmesis or possible clubfoot.3
On physical examination, metatarsus adductus is observed an adducted forefoot and a
curved lateral border, which, together, create the characteristic kidney bean–shaped
sole.3 The fifth metatarsal base may be prominent.3 The hindfoot is in neutral or a slight
valgus position, but it is never in a varus position.3 Range of motion of the ankle and
subtalar joints is normal.2 Hyperactivity of the abductor hallucis may contribute to the
dynamic component of the foot position, especially in patients younger than 18
months.2 An atavistic or wandering great toe (adduction of the great toe) also may be
observed.3 In addition, some patients have a mild plantar flexion deformity of the medial
column of the foot, resulting in the appearance of an elevated longitudinal arch.3
The flexibility of the deformity determines the prognosis and helps identify patients who
require treatment.3 Tickling the foot may reveal flexibility. Flexibility also can be assessed
by holding the hindfoot in a varus position to stabilize the subtalar joint and then
abducting the forefoot relative to the hindfoot. If the foot can be abducted fully, then the
heel-bisector line falls between the great toe and the second toe, indicating that the
deformity is fully flexible and likely will resolve spontaneously. The foot also may be
moderately flexible, whereby alignment improves with stress, but the heel-bisector line
cannot be brought in line with the second toe. Truly rigid deformities are rare. The
deformity may have a dynamic component from overactivity of the abductor hallucis,
which makes the condition more dramatic during walking.3
Later in life, patients with a rigid deformity that does not resolve may have concerns of
cosmesis, an in-toed gait, or excessive shoe wear. Pressure sites during shoe wear

9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Metatarsus Adductus and Calcaneovalgus Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000032
7/17

include medial border of first metatarsophalangeal joint or prominent lateral border at
the base of the fifth metatarsal.2
Radiographs rarely are necessary; however, they are indicated if a deformity cannot be
passively corrected or fails to respond to nonsurgical management. In such patients,
obliquity of the medial cuneiform in combination with adduction of the metatarsals at
the level of the tarsometatarsal joint may be present.3 In older children, medial deviation
of the metatarsal shafts may be observed.3
Parents may suspect clubfoot; however, clinical examination will reveal the absence of
hindfoot varus and ankle equinus. Several other diagnoses that are distinguishable from
metatarsus adductus should be considered. In patients with a hyperactive abductor
hallucis, the lateral border of the foot remains straight. In patients with internal tibial
torsion, the foot is rotated in and the lateral border of the foot is straight. A decreased
intermalleolar axis also will be observed. In patients with skewfoot, a Z-shaped or
serpentine foot with the hindfoot in valgus and the forefoot in adduction is
observed.3 Metatarsus adductus also must be distinguished from hallux varus secondary
to a bracket epiphysis and metatarsus primus varus, in which the lateral border of the
foot is normal but a medial crease occurs secondary to isolated varus alignment of the
first ray. This latter deformity typically is rigid, requires early cast immobilization, and
may contribute to a hallux valgus deformity of the great toe (Resource 2; Figure 3).

metatarsus adductus. (Reproduced from Lincoln TL, Suen PW: Common rotational
variations in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2003;11[5]:312-320.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Spontaneous resolution of metatarsus adductus occurs in 90% to 95% of children by age 4
years.
Passive stretching is recommended for patients with a flexible deformity but may not improve
the final outcome.
Serial cast immobilization of a rigid deformity is useful in children aged 6 to 12 months.
Surgical Management
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Metatarsus Adductus and Calcaneovalgus Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000032
9/17

Surgical treatment is indicated only in children older than 3 to 4 years who have a severe
residual deformity that causes pain or problems with shoe wear.
Techniques/Procedures
Medial column lengthening (opening wedge osteotomy of the cuneiform) in combination with
lateral column shortening (closing wedge of the cuboid)

Management
Flexible deformities may be managed via observation or stretching because 90% to 95%
will resolve spontaneously regardless of management.1 Dynamic deformities also
resolve on their own.3 Even without complete resolution, no evidence suggests that such
deformity causes pain in adulthood.2 In patients with a rigid deformity, serial
manipulation and cast immobilization may result in deformity correction in 6 to 8 weeks.
The cast should be applied in a manner in which the forefoot is held in abduction
without accentuating heel valgus. Complications of cast immobilization include increased
heel valgus and a flatfoot or skewfoot deformity. Cast immobilization should be
performed before age 6 months because it is less successful and is associated with a
higher failure rate in children aged 1 to 3 years. Nighttime splints and special shoes have
no proven value; however, they often are a supplement to cast immobilization in
patients with a structural deformity.3
Surgical treatment is indicated only in older children with a rigid deformity that has not
responded to serial cast immobilization and that results in painful shoe wear. Surgical
treatment options to manage soft-tissue tightness include abductor hallucis muscle
lengthening, medial midfoot capsulotomy, tarsometatarsal joint capsulotomy, and
release of the intermetatarsal ligaments.2 However, these soft-tissue procedures have
not been deemed successful, and degenerative changes at the tarsometatarsal joints
have been observed after soft-tissue releases of the tarsometatarsal joints.3
In patients older than 3 years, an opening wedge osteotomy of the medial cuneiform in
combination with a closing wedge osteotomy of the cuboid or osteotomies at the base of

the second through fourth metatarsals is safe and appears to be the most effective
surgical treatment option.2 Complications of osteotomies include undercorrection or
overcorrection. Damage to the physis of the first metatarsal, with subsequent shortening
of that bone, is a complication of a first metatarsal osteotomy.3
Other Complications
Damage to the physis of the first metatarsal, with subsequent shortening of the bone, is a
complication of a first metatarsal osteotomy.
Calcaneovalgus Foot
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
In newborns, a calcaneovalgus foot is the result of soft-tissue contractures.
No dislocation or bony deformity of the foot exists.
Calcaneovalgus foot is a positional deformity in infants, in which the foot is hyperdorsiflexed
secondary to intrauterine positioning (Figure 4).
More common in firstborn females
Figure 4 Clinical photograph shows a calcaneovalgus foot in a newborn. Note the characteristic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Metatarsus Adductus and Calcaneovalgus Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000032
11/17

hyperdorsiflexion and hindfoot valgus. (Reproduced from Sullivan JA: Pediatric flatfoot: Evaluation
and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1999;7[1]:44-53.)
Epidemiology
The estimated incidence of calcaneovalgus deformity is 0.4 to 1.0 in 1,000 live births.1
More common in girls, firstborn children, and children of young mothers.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Tendons
Tendons are normal in structure and location.
Musculotendinous units of the posterior and deep posterior compartments often are
elongated because of calcaneus and hindfoot valgus deformities.
Musculotendinous units of the anterior and lateral compartments often are contracted
because of calcaneus and hindfoot valgus deformities.
Joints and Ligaments
Hyperdorsiflexion is present through the tibiotalar joint.
Ankle joint morphology is normal.
Musculature
Muscle structure and function are normal.
Musculotendinous units of the posterior and deep posterior compartments often are
elongated because of calcaneus and hindfoot valgus deformities.
Musculotendinous units of the anterior and lateral compartments often are contracted
because of calcaneus and hindfoot valgus deformities.
Etiology
Intrauterine malpositioning is thought to cause this deformity.2


Etiology
Positional calcaneovalgus foot is a flexible deformity characterized by dorsiflexion at the
ankle and mild subtalar joint eversion. It is more common in girls, firstborn children, and
children of young mothers. Intrauterine malpositioning is thought to cause this
deformity.2 The estimated incidence of this deformity is 0.4 to 1.0 in 1,000 live births.1
Evaluation/Diagnosis
The deformity should be passively correctable to neutral.
May be associated with posteromedial bowing of the tibia; however, isolated posteromedial
tibial bowing may be misdiagnosed as a calcaneovalgus foot.
Physical Examination
The deformity is flexible.
The ankle is hyperdorsiflexed, often to the extent that the dorsum of the foot abuts the
anterior distal leg.
The heel is in a valgus position.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
In the absence of concern for posteromedial bowing of the tibia, radiographs are not
indicated.
Plain radiography is recommended to confirm a suspected diagnosis of posteromedial bowing
of the tibia.
Advanced imaging studies are not required. 
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is made via physical examination.
Characteristic positioning of the foot and flexibility usually are sufficient to make a diagnosis.

Radiographs may be used to confirm suspected posteromedial tibial bowing.
Differential Diagnosis
Isolated posteromedial bowing of the tibia
Congenital vertical talus
Congenital oblique talus
Flexible flatfoot deformity
Evaluation/Diagnosis

Evaluation/Diagnosis
On physical examination, the hindfoot externally rotates and dorsiflexes. In some
patients, the dorsum of the foot is in contact with the anterior tibia. A calcaneovalgus
foot must be distinguished from posteromedial bowing of the tibia with an apparent
calcaneovalgus foot. In patients with an isolated calcaneovalgus foot, the apex of the
deformity is in the ankle joint; in patients with posteromedial bowing, the apex of the
deformity is in the distal tibia1 (Figure 5). Calcaneovalgus foot also should be
differentiated from vertical talus by examining the hindfoot. In patients with a
calcaneovalgus foot, the calcaneus is dorsiflexed (in calcaneus), whereas in patients with
a vertical talus, the calcaneus is in equinus and, which gives the foot a characteristic
rocker bottom appearance.3
Imaging studies are not necessary for diagnosis but may help rule out a more serious
underlying disorder, such as congenital vertical talus or posteromedial bowing of the
tibia.2
The literature on the association between calcaneovalgus foot and DDH is conflicting;
however, DDH appears to be more likely in patients with calcaneovalgus in one foot and
metatarsus adductus in the contralateral foot.3

from posteromedial bowing. A, Photograph shows a calcaneovalgus deformity. Note that

Management
Calcaneovalgus foot typically resolves without management.
Stretching may expedite resolution but has no major effect on the natural history of
calcaneovalgus foot.

Management
Gentle stretching of the foot into plantar flexion and inversion may be helpful; however,
most deformities resolve spontaneously by age 3 to 6 months. In children with
posteromedial bowing of the tibia, parents should be counseled that a limb-length
discrepancy, usually 3 to 4 cm, is likely and surgical management may be required later
in life for limb-length equalization.1
